newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian budget seen boosting farm subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Indian budget seen boosting farm subsidies.

text.p: Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's promised support for farmers and pressure from his leftist allies are expected to result in higher agricultural subsidies in the federal budget, economists and analysts said on Sunday.

Analysts said a bout of competitive populism was in store in India's largely agrarian economy after a new local government in the agriculture-rich state of Punjab last week announced free electricity and water for farmers.

Rising farm subsidies have put pressure on government spending and pushed up the country's fiscal deficit. A deficit of 5.0 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is projected for the year to March 1997, against 5.9 percent in 1995/96.
"I don't expect much because there is a lot of pressure from the left on continuing subsidies," Anil Sharma, economist at the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) told Reuters.
Deve Gowda, a farmer turned politician, heads a 15-party alliance of regional, centrist and left-wing parties.
Soon after assuming office in June, Deve Gowda said as a peasant his priorities would be rural development and prominence to the agriculture sector.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is due to present the fiscal budget to parliament on February 28. Analysts said Chidambaram might make the budget as populist as possible to satisfy different sections in the fragile coalition.
The government has already raised the price of sugar sold through its retail outlets and the open market price of wheat in order to cut food subsidy.
"These have been taken care of before the budget and the budget would be made to appear soft," said one analyst.
India's food and fertiliser subsidies in the 1996/97 (April-March) budget are estimated at 127 billion rupees, with food accounting for 67 billion rupees.
"The political climate is such that the leftists want food subsidies to be increased," said Charan Wadhwa of the Centre for Policy Research. "The bill will go up both on food and fertiliser."
India had its ninth good monsoon in a row in 1996. Agriculture employs about two-thirds of India's workers and accounts for more than a third of its gross domestic product (GDP).
"I don't think there will be any reduction in subsidies. On the other hand they are thinking of raising subsidies like on potash," Sharma said.
The Indian government on Friday increased the price of urea fertiliser by 10 percent.
Sharma said the government was dithering over increasing the issue price of wheat and rice through the public distribution system (PDS).
He said government was also planning to implement a revised PDS, supplying 10 kg of foodgrains at half the issue price to about 45 million families below the poverty line.
Wadhwa said he did not expect any measures in the budget to boost foodgrains exports.

A foodgrains importer until the early 1980s, India has been exporting foodgrains after an increase in output to 190.4 million tonnes in 1995/96 (April-March) from 50.8 million in 1950-51. Production is estimated to rise to 191.18 million tonnes in 1996/97 from 185.04 million in 1995/96.
In December India decided to import two million tonnes of wheat, after a shortfall in production. It halted wheat exports in September.
